quote: Pyrgos is a typical example of medieval architecture with narrow, labyrinthine streets, fortified walls and hidden passages.

pirates.label: supported
pirates.says: In the 15th and 16th centuries pirates plundered harvests and enslaved people; islanders built villages at high, inaccessible points with outer walls without openings.
quote: During the 15th and 16th centuries, the Cyclades were under threat from pirates who plundered harvests and enslaved men and women to be sold in the slave markets.

the islanders built their settlements at the highest, most inaccessible points of the island, and very close to, or on top of, each other; their external walls, devoid of openings, formed a protective perimeter around the village.

five.label: supported
five.says: There were five kasteli on the island: Agios Nikolaos at Oia, Akrotiri, Emborio, Pyrgos and Skaros.
quote: Casteli (castles), also written as kasteli, were large, fortified, permanent settlements. There were five on the island: Agios Nikolaos (at Oia), Akrotiri, Emborio, Pyrgos, and Skaros.

theodosia.label: supported
theodosia.says: At the entrance to every kasteli was a church of St Theodosia, protector of castles.
quote: At the entrance to every casteli was a church dedicated to Agia (St.) Theodosia, the Protector-Saint of castles.

goulas.label: supported
goulas.says: A goulas was the highest tower of most kasteli, used as lookout and refuge, with thick walls and murder holes.
quote: Goulas (from the Turkish word kule which means 'tower') were multi-storey, rectangular, and the highest tower of most kastelli.
They were used both as observatories and as places of refuge for the islanders. They had thick walls, parapets, iron gates, murder holes, and embrasures.

kasteli.label: supported

quote: On top of this hill remain the ruins of a Venetian castle (Kasteli) that was once the island's administrative center.

the newest and best preserved is Pyrgos Castle

parts.name: Arrival
parts.stand: At the foot of the village, where the lanes start to climb toward the top of the hill.

paras.t: Welcome to Pyrgos. The name means Tower, and its full name, Pyrgos Kallistis, means Beauty Tower. The village wraps around this hill like an amphitheater, and it's one of the places on Santorini least spoiled by tourism.
We'll climb up through the lanes to the top. The steps and paving can be uneven, so take it slowly, and carry water. The sun here is strong.
It's a real village, not a stage set: 1,078 people lived here at the 2021 census, some 7 kilometers from Fira.

parts.name: The maze of lanes
parts.stand: Partway up, in one of the narrow lanes between the houses.

paras.t: Notice how the lanes twist and turn. Pyrgos is a classic medieval village, with narrow, maze-like streets, fortified walls and hidden passages.

There was a reason for the maze. In the 1400s and 1500s, pirates raided these islands, stealing harvests and carrying people off to be sold as slaves. So islanders built their villages on the highest, hardest-to-reach ground, with houses packed tightly together. The outer walls had no openings, so the village itself became a wall.

There were five of these fortified villages on the island, called kasteli: at Oia, Akrotiri, Emborio, Skaros, and here at Pyrgos. And every one had a church at its entrance dedicated to Saint Theodosia, the protector of castles.

parts.name: The Kasteli at the top
parts.stand: At the top of the village, beside the ruins of the old castle.

paras.t: Up here are the ruins of the Venetian castle, the Kasteli. For a time it was the administrative center of the whole island.

The Venetians conquered Santorini in 1207, and over the following centuries five fortified castles went up around the island. Of them, the castle at Pyrgos is the newest and the best preserved. It belonged to the same defense system as the castle at Oia.
Most of these castles had a goulas, a tall rectangular tower. It was a lookout and a last refuge, with thick walls, iron gates and murder holes, the openings for dropping things on attackers.

parts.name: The view
parts.stand: Find a spot at the top with a clear view out across the island.

paras.t: And now look around. From this hill you can see Santorini in almost every direction.

Here's something you might not guess. Most of Santorini is volcanic, but under it lies a small, older island that isn't. That old rock comes to the surface in just a few places, and Pyrgos is one of them. You're standing on the island before the volcano.

Up on the highest hill of the island, near Pyrgos, is the monastery of Profitis Ilias, the Prophet Elijah. It's rarely open to visitors. A walking trail starts just south of the village and passes it on the way to Kamari.

In the last years of Ottoman rule it was one of the most important monastic centers in the Cyclades. And in 1822, during the Greek War of Independence, sixteen of its monks, led by their abbot, Gerasimos Mavrommatis, declared in writing their support for the revolt.
And if you enjoy wine, there are local wineries you can visit in Pyrgos itself.

parts.name: Closing
parts.stand: Stay at the top for a moment before heading back down.

paras.t: Up here, the old walls guard nothing anymore, and anyone can wander in. Take your time going down. Let the twisting lanes slow you down; somebody once wanted them to, and they still do it well.
